subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Language Instinct
description: A 60-second lesson on The Language Instinct.

hook.text: Every healthy child on Earth learns language by age five without formal instruction. No exceptions.

buildup.text: Steven Pinker called language an instinct—not a cultural invention but a biological adaptation.

discovery.text: Children don't just memorize. They overgeneralize rules—saying 'goed' instead of 'went'—proving they extract grammar.

twist.text: Deaf children not exposed to sign language invent their own gestural grammar spontaneously.

climax.text: Language emerges like walking—you don't teach it. You just provide an environment and the brain does the rest.

punchline.text: You don't learn language—it grows in you.

quiz.question: What does children saying 'goed' instead of 'went' demonstrate?
options: They extract and apply grammatical rules

details.summary: Steven Pinker argues language is a biological instinct, not a cultural invention. Children acquire grammar effortlessly without formal instruction, often producing rules they never heard.
details.whyItMatters: The language instinct view reframes language acquisition as biology, not teaching. It explains why children master grammar before they master tying shoes.
takeaways: Children acquire grammar without explicit instruction
Dedicated brain areas support a language-specific capacity

faq.question: What evidence supports language as an instinct?
faq.answer: Children worldwide follow the same acquisition milestones regardless of culture. Creole languages emerge with full grammar from pidgins in one generation. Deaf children invent sign languages spontaneously. Specific genes like FOXP2 affect language ability.

faq.question: Do all linguists agree language is innate?
faq.answer: No. Usage-based theorists like Michael Tomasello argue children learn language through general cognitive abilities and social interaction, not a specialized instinct. They point to the role of input frequency and statistical learning.
